question: What happens to the glomeruli in chronic glomerulonephritis over time?

options.C: Nephrons grow larger and filter faster
options.D: Fibrous scar tissue replaces working kidney tissue

explanation: Chronic inflammation causes permanent damage, leading to fibrosis and the replacement of normal glomerular structures with scar tissue. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h1)

question: Why do people with chronic glomerulonephritis often feel fine in the early stages?

options.A: Urine output stops completely on day one
options.B: Healthy nephrons work harder to make up for damaged ones over years
options.C: Blood pressure stays very low until total failure happens
options.D: Symptoms only show up after eating heavy protein

explanation: The slow progression allows compensatory mechanisms in remaining nephrons to maintain balance until severe damage accumulates. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h1)

question: Which cells in the kidney produce the extra proteins that cause scarring in the glomerulus?
explanation: Inflammatory stimulation causes mesangial cells to multiply and overproduce matrix proteins, leading to scarring of the glomerulus. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h2)

question: How does immune damage lead to a lower kidney filtration rate?

options.A: Antibodies push extra water out into the tubules
options.B: White blood cells block the ureter completely
options.C: Inflammation and scarring narrow the tiny blood vessels and slow blood flow
options.D: The renal pelvis reabsorbs all filtered fluid

explanation: Immune injury triggers cellular proliferation and fibrosis, which physically narrows the filtering capillaries and drops the filtration rate. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h2)

question: Which of these long-term body conditions can lead to chronic kidney damage?
explanation: Sustained high blood pressure damages the delicate blood vessels within the kidneys, accelerating the loss of functional glomeruli. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which condition is NOT a common cause of chronic glomerulonephritis?
explanation: Pneumonia affects the respiratory system primarily and is not a direct primary cause of chronic glomerular injury. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h3)

question: What is a common sign you might see on a patient's face in the morning when they lose protein through their urine?
explanation: Hypoalbuminemia reduces plasma oncotic pressure, frequently manifesting as swelling around the eyes upon waking. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why do patients with advanced chronic kidney disease often develop anemia?

options.A: Frequent hospital blood tests drain all iron
options.B: Uremic toxins destroy platelets in the blood
options.C: Strict diets stop vitamin C absorption
options.D: Damaged kidneys stop making enough erythropoietin hormone

explanation: The failing kidneys lose their endocrine function, failing to signal the bone marrow to produce sufficient red blood cells. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h4)

question: What would an ultrasound scan show that points to chronic kidney disease rather than an acute injury?

options.C: Small, shrunken kidneys on both sides

explanation: Chronic disease causes extensive fibrosis and tissue loss, resulting in visibly smaller kidneys on imaging. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why might a doctor skip doing a kidney biopsy in very late-stage chronic kidney disease?

options.A: Ultrasound is always better at showing cell details
options.B: The procedure causes permanent vision loss
options.C: Blood urea must be zero for local anesthesia to work
options.D: Too much scarring makes it impossible to tell what caused the original damage

explanation: When nephrons are completely replaced by scar tissue, the specific original cause is often obscured beyond recognition. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which medication group is often given to lower pressure inside the glomerulus and reduce protein in the urine?
explanation: ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arterioles more than afferent arterioles, lowering pressure within the glomerulus and reducing protein leak. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the main reason for cutting down on dietary protein in chronic kidney disease?

options.A: To keep blood albumin high and prevent clots
options.B: To help the basement membrane grow back fast
options.C: To lower the buildup of nitrogen waste products in the blood

explanation: Lowering protein intake reduces the burden of metabolizing nitrogen, easing symptoms of uremia and protecting remaining nephrons. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the most accurate way to check daily fluid balance in a patient with chronic kidney disease?

options.A: Counting how many times they urinate
options.D: Measuring arm size with a tape

explanation: Weighing the patient daily under standard conditions provides the most reliable data on acute fluid retention or loss. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h7)

question: Why must patients with kidney failure avoid eating too much potassium?

options.A: Potassium causes severe swelling around the eyes
options.B: Damaged kidneys cannot clear potassium well, which can cause dangerous heart rhythms
options.C: Potassium stops blood pressure medications from working
options.D: High potassium destroys red blood cells instantly

explanation: Impaired glomerular filtration leads to potassium retention, which can cause fatal heart rhythm disturbances if dietary intake is not controlled. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the final stage of chronic kidney disease that requires dialysis or a transplant called?
explanation: When nephron destruction is nearly complete, the condition is termed end-stage renal disease, requiring dialysis or transplantation. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h8)

question: Why do patients in late-stage kidney failure often develop metabolic acidosis?

options.A: The liver makes too much lactic acid from a poor diet
options.B: The kidneys fail to clear hydrogen ions and keep enough bicarbonate
options.C: Drinking less water makes glucose ferment in the bladder
options.D: High blood pressure pushes acid out into body tissues

explanation: Damaged nephrons lose their ability to regulate acid-base balance, leading to an accumulation of hydrogen ions and depletion of buffers. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T5#GNS213_U4_T5_h8)
